label: adaptive-model-comparison
note: Illustrative stated starting points; live provider calls, no user Chart writes.

context.intention: I maintain a consistent workout routine.
context.actualStartingPoint: I exercise sporadically. I can use three 30-minute slots each week for bodyweight exercise at home.
context.destinationDescription: I maintain a consistent workout routine.

raw.destination: I maintain a consistent workout routine

waypoints.title: Use all three weekly workout slots
waypoints.rationale: A consistent routine starts with showing up in each available slot.
waypoints.completionCriteria: Each of the three 30-minute home workout slots is used for exercise in a typical week.

moves.title: Schedule the three slots in advance
moves.rationale: Turning the available time into fixed appointments makes the routine more likely to happen.

moves.title: Do a short bodyweight session in the next open slot
moves.rationale: This converts intention into an actual workout inside the current constraints.

moves.title: Repeat the same workout pattern for the remaining slots this week
moves.rationale: Repeating a simple format reduces decision-making and supports consistency.

waypoints.title: Complete workouts without needing extra setup
waypoints.rationale: The routine becomes reliable when starting a session is straightforward and repeatable.
waypoints.completionCriteria: A workout can begin and finish at home within 30 minutes using bodyweight exercises only, without extra preparation getting in the way.

moves.title: Use one fixed warm-up sequence before each session
moves.rationale: A repeatable start helps each workout feel automatic.

moves.title: Keep one simple workout template for all three sessions
moves.rationale: A consistent template removes the need to decide what to do each time.

moves.title: Set out clothes or clear space before the session starts
moves.rationale: Reducing friction makes it easier to begin on time.

waypoints.title: Hold the routine across a full week
waypoints.rationale: Consistency is established when the pattern survives normal weekly distractions.
waypoints.completionCriteria: The three weekly sessions are completed for a full week without one being skipped.

moves.title: Treat the three slots as non-negotiable appointments for one week
moves.rationale: This tests whether the routine can hold under a normal schedule.

moves.title: If one slot is missed, move it to the next available same-week slot
moves.rationale: This keeps the weekly pattern intact instead of dropping the session entirely.

moves.title: Review which part of the week caused the most friction
moves.rationale: Learning the failure point helps protect the routine next week.

suggestedOneMove.title: Schedule the three slots in advance
suggestedOneMove.rationale: Locking the available time into the week is the smallest concrete step toward consistency.

raw.personalizedGuidance: Given your 3 weekly 30-minute home slots, the first stretch is simply using them consistently rather than adding more volume.

analysis.startingPointSummary: The person already has three 30-minute home slots each week and currently exercises sporadically.
assumptions: Bodyweight exercise at home is feasible without extra equipment.
The goal is routine consistency, not a specific performance target.
Three weekly slots are the relevant available structure to build on.
analysis.firstMilestoneEvidence: A full week in which each of the three available slots is used for a workout.
analysis.difficultyReduction: The first milestone focuses on using the existing slots, not on intensity, progression, or longer sessions.

context.intention: I successfully complete my first half marathon.
context.actualStartingPoint: I run 5 km comfortably twice a week. I can train three days each week. I have never completed a half marathon.
context.destinationDescription: I successfully complete my first half marathon.

waypoints.title: Handle 8 km without strain
waypoints.rationale: This shows your body can stay controlled beyond your current 5 km base.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You can run 8 km at an easy, steady effort and finish without needing a recovery day beyond normal tiredness.

moves.title: Extend one weekly run to 6 km
moves.rationale: A small distance increase is the safest first step from your current routine.

moves.title: Add a second longer run at 7 km the following week
moves.rationale: This checks that the longer distance is repeatable, not a one-off.

moves.title: Complete one easy 8 km run
moves.rationale: This confirms you can cover the first major jump toward half-marathon distance.

waypoints.title: Run 10 km comfortably
waypoints.rationale: A 10 km run shows you can hold effort through the middle of the race distance.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You can run 10 km at an easy pace with stable form and predictable recovery.

moves.title: Make one weekly run 9 km
moves.rationale: This bridges the gap between 8 km and 10 km without a large jump.

moves.title: Repeat a 9 km run on a second week
moves.rationale: Repeating the distance shows the load is manageable in your routine.

moves.title: Complete one 10 km easy run
moves.rationale: This establishes a solid middle-distance base for longer training.

waypoints.title: Finish a 14 km long run
waypoints.rationale: This is the point where your body starts learning race-length endurance.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You complete a 14 km long run at an easy effort with no need to stop early.

moves.title: Stretch your long run to 12 km
moves.rationale: This is the next manageable step after 10 km.

moves.title: Repeat 12 km with the same easy effort
moves.rationale: Repeating the distance reduces the chance of treating it as a one-time peak.

moves.title: Complete one 14 km long run
moves.rationale: This shows you can handle most of the half-marathon distance in training.

waypoints.title: Complete a 16 km long run
waypoints.rationale: You need one more endurance step before race day feels routine rather than aspirational.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You finish a 16 km easy long run and recover normally over the next day or two.

moves.title: Plan one 15 km long run
moves.rationale: A small increase keeps the progression realistic.

moves.title: Repeat the 15 km run on another week
moves.rationale: This helps confirm the distance is sustainable.

moves.title: Complete one 16 km long run
moves.rationale: This gives you confidence that race day is within reach.

waypoints.title: Complete a full half marathon attempt
waypoints.rationale: This is the first real finish-line rehearsal at race distance.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You complete 21.1 km in an organised run or race, even if the pace is slower than planned.

moves.title: Choose a specific event or solo route of 21.1 km
moves.rationale: A defined attempt turns the goal into something concrete.

moves.title: Taper your longest run before the attempt
moves.rationale: Reducing fatigue helps you arrive ready to finish.

moves.title: Run the full distance and cross the finish line
moves.rationale: This is the final state the intention is aiming for.

suggestedOneMove.title: Extend one weekly run to 6 km
suggestedOneMove.rationale: It is the smallest concrete change that starts moving your current 5 km base toward half-marathon distance.

raw.personalizedGuidance: You already run twice a week, so this route starts by extending one run before building the long run and race-distance endurance.

analysis.startingPointSummary: The person can currently run 5 km comfortably twice a week and has capacity for three training days weekly, with no prior half-marathon finish.
assumptions: Training remains limited to three days per week as stated.
No extra equipment, coaching, or injury history is assumed.
The route should reflect observable running capacity and routine changes, not a generic training plan.
analysis.firstMilestoneEvidence: The first meaningful change is the ability to run beyond the current comfortable 5 km distance without strain, demonstrated by an 8 km easy run.
analysis.difficultyReduction: The first completion criterion is reduced from race completion to a modest extension of current distance, keeping the first step feasible from the stated baseline.

context.actualStartingPoint: Anchor is launched with 20 paying users. I am the solo developer, with 10 hours a week for growth and no paid advertising budget. I can contact current users and have subscription analytics.

vision.title: A sustainable Anchor business
vision.description: 10,000 paying users who continue using Anchor

raw.destination: Anchor has 10,000 paying users who continue using it

waypoints.title: Understand why the first users stay
waypoints.rationale: Retention evidence is the first test of whether the product is worth scaling.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You have a clear retention read on the current paid users and the main reasons they keep or stop using Anchor.
requirements: A simple retention snapshot for current paying users is reviewed
Top reasons for continued use are identified from user contact or analytics
Top reasons for churn or inactivity are identified
One retention problem is chosen as the next priority

moves.title: Review current subscription behavior
moves.rationale: Use the analytics you already have to see who is active, renewing, or dropping off.

moves.title: Message current paying users
moves.rationale: Ask a small set of users why they keep paying and what nearly caused them to leave.

moves.title: Group the answers into themes
moves.rationale: Turn scattered feedback into a short list of retention drivers and blockers.

moves.title: Pick one retention issue to fix first
moves.rationale: Focus the next changes on the biggest reason people stay or leave.

waypoints.title: Improve the paid user experience
waypoints.rationale: Better retention makes growth more durable before you push for more users.
waypoints.completionCriteria: The main retention issue is addressed in the product or onboarding and current users see a clearer reason to continue.
requirements: The chosen retention issue is fixed or reduced in the product
Users can reach the core value with less friction
At least one improvement is visible to current paying users
Follow-up feedback shows the change is understood or used

moves.title: Make the smallest product change that removes friction
moves.rationale: Start with the simplest fix tied to the retention problem.

moves.title: Update onboarding or prompts around the core value
moves.rationale: Help users reach the outcome that keeps them paying.

moves.title: Tell current users about the improvement
moves.rationale: Reconnect them to the value and invite them to use the change.

moves.title: Check whether the change is reducing complaints or drop-off
moves.rationale: Confirm the fix is actually improving retention behavior.

waypoints.title: See repeatable retention in the numbers
waypoints.rationale: A business can scale only after retention is strong enough to support acquisition.
waypoints.completionCriteria: A larger paid base is holding together over time, with the retention trend visible in subscription analytics.

moves.title: Track paying users by cohort or month
moves.rationale: Use the analytics you already have to see whether users stay after signing up.

moves.title: Compare the current group to earlier users
moves.rationale: Look for improvement after the retention fix rather than a one-time spike.

moves.title: Keep the retention-improving change in the product
moves.rationale: Hold onto the change that is helping users remain active and paying.

moves.title: Use the retention pattern to decide when to push acquisition harder
moves.rationale: Only scale further once the numbers show the product can hold users.

waypoints.title: Find one repeatable acquisition channel
waypoints.rationale: Growth needs a way to bring in new paying users without paid ads.
waypoints.completionCriteria: You have one acquisition method you can repeat manually with a predictable enough flow of new paying users.
requirements: One acquisition source is identified as promising
A repeatable outreach or distribution process exists
At least one message or channel variant is tested
The channel produces new paying users from a repeatable effort

moves.title: List acquisition sources available without ads
moves.rationale: Use the channels you can actually run as a solo developer with limited time.

moves.title: Test the simplest outreach or content version
moves.rationale: Start with the lowest-effort version that can reach potential users.

moves.title: Keep the version that brings the best response
moves.rationale: Repeat what converts instead of trying many channels at once.

moves.title: Document the steps needed to run the channel weekly
moves.rationale: Make it feasible to repeat inside 10 hours a week.

waypoints.title: Convert more of the right users into paid accounts
waypoints.rationale: A repeatable channel only matters if it reliably creates paying customers.
waypoints.completionCriteria: More users are paying through the repeatable channel, and the increase is visible in subscription analytics.

moves.title: Send traffic to the current subscription path
moves.rationale: Put the repeatable channel in front of the existing offer.

moves.title: Remove obvious signup or payment friction
moves.rationale: Help interested users finish the step from interest to payment.

moves.title: Watch where interested users stop
moves.rationale: Use the analytics to see which step blocks conversion.

moves.title: Refine the message or offer based on real responses
moves.rationale: Improve conversion without inventing a new business model.

waypoints.title: Scale without losing retention
waypoints.rationale: 10,000 paying users only matters if the business stays healthy as it grows.
waypoints.completionCriteria: Anchor reaches 10,000 paying users and the users continue using it at a durable level.

moves.title: Increase acquisition only after retention holds
moves.rationale: Avoid scaling a leaky base.

moves.title: Keep the repeatable channel running consistently
moves.rationale: Growth needs ongoing input, not one-off spikes.

moves.title: Monitor retention as the user base grows
moves.rationale: Make sure growth does not weaken product value.

moves.title: Expand only when the current system still holds together
moves.rationale: Use the same proven loop as the base gets larger.

suggestedOneMove.title: Message current paying users
suggestedOneMove.rationale: Ask a small set of users why they keep paying and what nearly caused them to leave.

raw.personalizedGuidance: Focus first on retention and a repeatable acquisition path; with no ad budget, scale has to come from what current users and a manual channel can prove.

analysis.startingPointSummary: Anchor is already launched, with 20 paying users, subscription analytics, 10 hours a week for growth, and no paid advertising budget.
assumptions: Current paying users are reachable for direct feedback
Subscription analytics are sufficient to observe retention patterns
Growth work must fit within 10 hours a week
No new budget will be used for paid acquisition
analysis.firstMilestoneEvidence: The first real change is understanding why paid users stay or leave, because that determines what to improve before trying to scale.
analysis.difficultyReduction: The first waypoint is narrowed to a clear retention read, not full optimization. The smallest next action is to contact current users, which uses available resources and does not require new tools or money.
